items.title: The Work of a Seed Bank
items.passage:
A seed bank preserves plant material so that future growers can recover varieties that have disappeared from ordinary cultivation. Its purpose differs from that of a grain warehouse: stored seeds must remain capable of producing living plants. Staff therefore test a sample from each collection before deciding how to store it.
Many crop seeds tolerate drying and low temperatures. These treatments slow the chemical reactions associated with aging, allowing seeds to remain viable for years. However, a freezer is not a permanent solution. Periodic germination tests reveal whether a collection is losing its ability to sprout. When that happens, staff grow new plants and collect a fresh generation of seeds.
Regeneration creates its own difficulty. If only a few plants reproduce, some of the original genetic diversity may be lost. Banks must grow enough individuals and prevent unwanted pollen from nearby varieties from reaching them. Detailed records identify where each sample originated and how it has been maintained.
Not every species can be conserved by this method. Some tropical seeds are damaged by drying. Living collections and other preservation techniques are needed for those plants. Seed banking is consequently one part of a broader conservation strategy, rather than a substitute for protecting plants in their natural habitats.

items.title: Reading a River’s Past
items.passage:
A river seldom follows one unchanging path across a plain. Over decades, bends migrate as water removes sediment from one bank and deposits it on another. Eventually a river may abandon a bend entirely. Although vegetation can hide the old channel, traces of it remain in the landscape.
Researchers combine several kinds of evidence to reconstruct these earlier routes. Aerial photographs may reveal curved lines in fields because plants grow differently above buried sand and clay. Historical maps offer another view, but their accuracy varies. A map produced to define property boundaries may represent a channel more carefully than one drawn primarily to show roads.
Sediment cores provide a way to investigate features that photographs only suggest. A core is a narrow column of material extracted from the ground. Coarse sand at one depth and fine mud above it can indicate a change from flowing water to a quieter environment. Dating suitable material helps establish when that change occurred.
No single clue determines the whole story. A curved mark could have another origin, and a core represents only a small location. Agreement among photographs, maps and several cores makes an interpretation stronger. Reconstructing past channels is useful beyond historical curiosity: former riverbeds can influence where floodwater moves and where buildings encounter unstable ground.

lower.title: Why Museums Rest Some Objects
lower.passage:
Visitors sometimes assume that an object absent from a museum gallery has been judged unimportant. In fact, rotating objects can be essential to their preservation. Light provides a clear example. It allows visitors to see an object, but exposure can also change the materials from which the object is made.
Colored textiles and works on paper are particularly vulnerable. Light can break chemical bonds in dyes, gradually changing their appearance. The effect depends on both brightness and duration. A moderate light level sustained for many months may cause more damage than a brief period of stronger illumination. Conservators therefore consider cumulative exposure rather than brightness alone.
Putting an object in darkness does not reverse fading that has already happened. A rest period instead limits the additional damage it receives. Museums may display one textile for a short season and replace it with another while keeping environmental conditions carefully controlled. Digital reproductions sometimes remain available when the original is in storage.
Rotation also creates a communication problem. A visitor who has traveled to see a famous piece may be disappointed. Explaining the conservation schedule helps visitors understand the decision. The museum must balance access now against the possibility of access in the future. Displaying everything continuously would maximize immediate visibility while potentially diminishing what future visitors could experience.

higher.prompt: What is the author’s main point?
options: Scientific models should contain every observable variable
A failed prediction can guide useful improvements in a scientific model

Models of lakes cannot produce useful predictions
higher.explanation: The passage presents failure as evidence for investigation and revision.
higher.title: Learning from an Unsuccessful Prediction
higher.passage:
Scientific models are simplified accounts of how a system behaves. A model might predict when a lake will develop an algal bloom using measurements of temperature and nutrients. If a bloom occurs earlier than predicted, the discrepancy does not by itself show that modeling is useless. It can instead identify something important that the model leaves out.
Researchers first examine the observations. A faulty instrument or an irregular sampling schedule may produce an apparent mismatch. If the measurements are dependable, they investigate the assumptions connecting those measurements to the predicted event. For example, mixing caused by wind might bring nutrients to the surface even when average nutrient measurements remain low.
Adding more variables is not automatically an improvement. A model can become so closely fitted to one set of observations that it performs poorly on new data. Researchers therefore reserve independent observations for testing. A useful revision should explain the initial failure while retaining its ability to make predictions beyond that particular case.
This process gives unsuccessful predictions a productive role. They help distinguish incomplete explanations from failures in measurement, and they suggest new observations to collect. A model earns confidence through repeated testing across circumstances, not simply through the number of details it contains or its success in describing events that are already known.

items.title: Detecting a Change in a Population

stimulus.title: Detecting a Change in a Population
stimulus.script:
Imagine counting insects beside a path every afternoon. One week your count drops sharply. Has the population declined? Perhaps, but first consider what else changed. If the second week was colder, insects may simply have been less active and therefore harder to observe. The count measures the animals detected, not automatically every animal present.
Ecologists call attention to detectability for exactly this reason. They may repeat observations at several times, record weather conditions, or use more than one survey method. Agreement between independent methods can make an explanation more convincing. However, adding methods is useful only when researchers understand how each one samples the population.
Here is another complication. Suppose your path runs beside flowers that finish blooming halfway through the study. Insects may move to another patch without leaving the wider area. A local count could fall even if the regional population remains stable. Expanding the survey to several habitats helps test that possibility.
The lesson is not that counts tell us nothing. They are often indispensable. But interpreting a change requires separating changes in abundance, activity and location. Careful records of survey conditions help future researchers judge which explanation the evidence actually supports.

items.title: Public Space after Sunset

stimulus.title: Public Space after Sunset
stimulus.script:
Today I want to consider a familiar place at an unfamiliar time. A city square can be busy at noon and almost empty after sunset. That difference may reflect lighting, transport schedules or the activities permitted there. We should not assume that its daytime use tells us everything about its role in the city.
Researchers studying public space sometimes conduct observations at several periods rather than choosing only convenient office hours. They note not just how many people are present but what people do and whether particular groups seem absent. Interviews can then explore why someone avoids the space at night. Perhaps the last bus leaves too early, or the route to the square feels uncomfortable.
Lighting can help, but brighter is not automatically better. A very bright area beside a dark passage can make the contrast difficult for pedestrians. Design needs to consider the whole route rather than an isolated lamp. Nearby evening activities may also contribute to a sense that the place is actively used.
So, when evaluating a public square, think about a sequence of experiences over time. The goal is not simply to reproduce the noon crowd after dark. It is to understand which conditions support people who would like to use the space then.

stimulus.script:
Some materials return toward a previous shape when conditions change. You may have encountered a demonstration in which a bent metal wire straightens when warmed. It looks as though the wire remembers being straight, although memory here is a description of material behavior rather than a mental process.
The explanation involves the internal arrangement of the material. Under one set of conditions, its structure can change in a way that permits deformation. Heating can favor a different arrangement, producing a return toward the earlier form. This behavior depends on the material and on staying within particular operating limits. You cannot assume that bending any metal and heating it will produce the same result.

options: Why interview recordings need no supporting information

higher.explanation: The speaker discusses questioning, interpretation and documentation.
higher.title: What Makes an Oral History Useful

stimulus.title: What Makes an Oral History Useful
stimulus.script:
An oral-history interview is not simply a container of facts waiting to be collected. It is an interaction between a person recalling experience and another person asking questions. The interviewer’s wording can influence which parts of a story receive attention and how the speaker explains them.
Consider the difference between asking whether a neighborhood project was successful and asking what changed after it began. The first question may encourage a simple judgment. The second leaves more room for the interviewee to describe mixed outcomes. Neither wording automatically produces a complete account, but they create different opportunities for elaboration.
Historians also distinguish a remembered experience from an exact record of an event. Someone may recall an incident clearly but place it in the wrong year. Comparing the interview with letters or newspapers can help establish chronology without making the personal account worthless. The way an event is remembered may itself be historically significant.
Finally, recordings need context. The date, circumstances and permissions associated with an interview affect how later researchers can use it. Preserving the sound without preserving this information would leave important questions unanswered. A useful oral history therefore combines the interview, responsible questioning and documentation that explains how the account came into being.
